expectations: wants pain relief and to know when headache is dangerous
social_hx: works night shifts, sleeps irregularly, no smoking

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Migraine is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Assess red flags, acute analgesia/triptan suitability, trigger diary, sleep advice, safety-net for sudden severe headache or neurological deficits, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: recurrent headaches with nausea

Key HPI features: throbbing unilateral headaches for 6 months, 2-3 times per month, nausea and light sensitivity, lasts several hours, better in a dark room, no weakness, no fever, no sudden thunderclap onset
Objective/Exam findings: Neurological exam, fundoscopy if indicated, headache diary.
Current medications: paracetamol occasionally, no regular medications
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Migraine.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Tension headache without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Sudden thunderclap onset, fever, or new neurological deficit — would suggest a secondary cause instead.
management_principles: Assess red flags, acute analgesia/triptan suitability, trigger diary, sleep advice, safety-net for sudden severe headache or neurological deficits
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
Provide clear patient education, address patient concerns, and establish explicit follow-up and safety-netting instructions.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 29F with recurrent unilateral throbbing headaches with nausea and photophobia, no red flag symptoms reported.
reference_soap.objective: Neurological exam, fundoscopy if indicated, headache diary.
reference_soap.assessment: Migraine likely. DDx: tension headache, medication-overuse headache; red flags less likely from history.
reference_soap.plan: Assess red flags, acute analgesia/triptan suitability, trigger diary, sleep advice, safety-net for sudden severe headache or neurological deficits.

learning_objectives: Explain migraine and safety-net symptoms in patient language

teaching.one_liner: Recurrent throbbing, one-sided headaches with nausea and light sensitivity, lasting hours and relieved in a dark room — the diagnosis rests on the recurring pattern, and treatment includes both acute relief and trigger identification.
red_flags: Sudden thunderclap onset, fever, or new neurological deficit — would suggest a secondary cause instead

must_ask.say: Is the pain throbbing and on one side of your head?
Do you feel nauseated or sensitive to light during the headache?
How often do these happen, and how long do they last?
Does resting in a dark room help?
What worries you most about these headaches?

history.answer: I have been having bad headaches that keep coming back, and they make me feel really nauseated.
It builds up slowly over one or two hours, not like a sudden explosion or lightning bolt.
These started about six months ago and happen two or three times a month. The pattern has stayed about the same since it began.
It is usually on one side of my head, right around my right temple and behind my right eye.
It feels like a throbbing, pounding ache, and the pain reaches around a seven out of ten.
Each episode lasts anywhere from four to eight hours. It does not wake me up in the middle of the night or right when I open my eyes in the morning.
Walking around or bending over makes the throbbing much worse. Resting in a quiet, dark room helps take the edge off.
No, I do not see flashing lights, zigzags, or blind spots before the headache starts, and I do not get any tingling.
I feel very nauseated during the attacks, though I have not actually vomited. Bright lights and loud noises bother me terribly.
No, my eye does not tear up or turn red, my nose does not run, and my eyelid does not droop.
No, I have not had any fever, stiff neck, or skin rashes.
No, I have not had any weakness in my arms or legs, numbness, slurred speech, confusion, or seizures.
No, my vision has been completely normal, with no blurry vision, double vision, or eye pain.
No, I have not had any recent head injuries, bumps, or falls.
I take paracetamol occasionally, maybe two or three days a month. It takes the edge off slightly, but the throbbing usually persists.
Working irregular night shifts and missing sleep seem to trigger the attacks, as does heavy stress. I have not noticed specific food triggers.
No, I do not have high blood pressure, and I do not take blood pressure medications or blood thinners.
No one else living with me has headaches, and we do not use any indoor gas heaters.
No, I have never had cancer, HIV, or taken medications that suppress the immune system.
I read a bit online and wondered if this might be migraines, since the throbbing and light sensitivity seem similar.
I am really worried that this might be caused by something dangerous, like a brain tumor.
I want to find a medicine that actually stops the pain, and I want to know what warning signs mean a headache is dangerous.
I do not have any chronic illnesses or major medical conditions.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
Only paracetamol once in a while for bad headaches. I do not take any regular prescription medicines or supplements.
No, I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or anything else.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink socially, maybe a glass of beer once or twice a month.
I work night shifts at a manufacturing facility and live alone in an apartment.
My mother gets migraines, but no one in my family has had a brain tumor, aneurysm, or stroke.
My last period started two weeks ago, and my menstrual cycles are regular every twenty-eight days.
My partner and I use condoms. My home pregnancy test last month was negative, and there is no chance I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.6 °C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, attentive, and fully oriented to person, place, and time with fluent speech.
Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light; visual fields full to confrontation; fundoscopy shows sharp optic disc margins without papilledema.
Cranial nerves II through XII intact bilaterally with normal extraocular movements and symmetric facial expression.
Normal muscle bulk and tone with 5/5 strength throughout all four extremities.
Intact light touch and pinprick sensation bilaterally across all extremities and trunk.
Biceps, triceps, patellar, and Achilles deep tendon reflexes 2+ bilaterally; Babinski sign absent bilaterally.
Finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements intact; gait is steady and Romberg test is negative.
Supple neck with full active and passive flexion; negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
No tenderness on palpation or percussion over the frontal or maxillary sinuses.
Full cervical spine range of motion without paraspinal muscle spasm or tenderness.
